title: The emotional influence of different geometries in virtual spaces: A neurocognitive examination
research_question: How do geometric criteria (protrusion, curvature, scale, and proportion) in virtual architectural spaces influence human emotional and cognitive reactions, as measured by physiological, behavioral, and self-report methods?

participants.description: 45 male (M=27.82, SD=5.46), 67 female (M=26.54, SD=5.27). Age range 21-46 years. 12 designers (M=33.8, SD=5.72) and 100 non-designers (M=26.24, SD=4.73). Exclusions: ADHD, visual deficits (uncorrected), heart disease, pregnancy, vertigo, claustrophobia.
participants.recruitment: Advertisements published on the web, in social media, and by word-of-mouth.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 27 virtual 3D models (scenes) with varying degrees of protrusion (P=0,4), curvature (C=0,4), scale (S=1,3), and proportion (height P(H): H1,H1b,H2,H3; width P(W): W1,W1b,W2,W3). Generated using Grasshopper plugin for Rhino and exported to Unity real-time engine. Experienced via HTC Vive VR headset.

implementation_implications: Implications for residential, education, and rehabilitation settings are evidenced.
Designing large spaces is a commonly used technique to create a dramatic effect and gain a sense of awe.
Large spaces are suitable for multitudes, not only due to their large capacity but also due to their tendency to attract participants to stay in those spaces longer.
To design spaces which create a high level of excitement, extreme proportions or scale may be used.
Narrow spaces are experienced significantly more often as distressing.
Design more affectively sympathetic spaces with potential applications for special needs children, educational structures, geriatric and rehabilitation spaces, public and living spaces.

tables.description: Analysis of emotional response upon recognition of a VS, summarizing physiological and human-centered measurable variables and geometrical space criteria.

limitations: Inability to precisely evaluate measures according to their relative contribution to the total variance.
Difficulty in determining the actual contribution of dominant measures (e.g., high FD and high βBP).
Difficulty in distinguishing if negative emotion is easier to recognize or if physiology is more engaged in signaling negative emotions.
The study used limited parametric change in form and specific participant orientation towards VSs.
Impossibility to attach a single measurement to a specific emotional state.
